opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been really fun to watch. When we built it, we mostly had knowledge workers in mind: people doing market research, literature reviews, that kind of thing. A lot of people do use it that way. But some of my favorite uses have been much more personal.

A lot of people use it for shopping. If you're buying something with many options and tradeoffs, like a car, a stroller, or an appliance, it'll go read every review and spec sheet and come back with a comparison. That's tedious for a person and well suited to the model. Travel planning is similar. People ask for really specific itineraries with lots of constraints, and it handles those surprisingly well.

Medical questions have been striking too. People use it to understand a diagnosis that they or a family member received, or to dig into recent research on a rare condition. We've heard really touching stories from people who said it helped them go into a doctor's appointment better informed and ask better questions. Obviously it's not a replacement for a doctor, but it can be really empowering.

Coding has been another one. People have it look through documentation and figure out how to use a library or an API, even though that wasn't what we were optimizing for.

And then there's the fun, niche stuff: people researching their family history, digging into some obscure hobby, or just going down a rabbit hole they've been curious about for years. That's been the most delightful part for me. When you give people a tool that can spend real time on a question, they bring all kinds of questions to it that you'd never have predicted.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that surprised me most is how much people use it for very personal stuff, not just work research. I'd expected the finance analysts, the people doing market research, the scientists doing literature reviews, and we definitely see a lot of that. But then we started hearing from people who were using it for things like planning a very specific trip, where they had a lot of constraints, like they wanted to go to a certain region, they had dietary restrictions, they had kids of a certain age, and it would go and find these very niche blogs and forums that you would never find with a normal search.

Shopping is another one that I didn't expect to be as big as it is. People doing really thorough comparisons when they're buying a car or a bike or some appliance, where they actually care about getting it right and are willing to wait the five or twenty minutes for a really complete answer. That tradeoff, where you give up speed for depth, turns out to apply to a lot more everyday decisions than I assumed.

And then there's the medical and health use cases, which I think have been both surprising and really meaningful. People researching a diagnosis a family member got, trying to understand the latest clinical trials, trying to figure out what questions to ask their doctor. Those are the ones where you get the emails from people saying it genuinely changed how they approached a conversation, and that's been really motivating for the team.

The other thing I'd call out is coding. We didn't position it as a coding tool at all, but people use it to research unfamiliar libraries or figure out how to approach a migration, basically reading all the docs and GitHub issues for them before they start. I think the common thread is that whenever a task requires reading a lot of sources and synthesizing them, people find it, even if we never thought of that domain ourselves.

astra-6.text:
One thing that’s surprised me is how useful it is for personal decisions. You hear “deep research” and think of scientific papers or detailed industry reports, but choosing where to go on vacation or figuring out what to buy can involve a lot of research, too.

The interesting part is being able to give it your particular constraints and preferences. You’re not just asking, “What’s the best product?” You’re asking, “What’s the best product for me, given all these things I care about?” It can work through those trade-offs and give you something much more useful than a generic list.

sol-6.1.text: One thing that’s surprised me is how useful it is for everyday decisions. You might think of it as a tool for writing a detailed research report, but people also want help figuring out what to buy, planning a trip, or navigating a complicated personal decision. Those tasks involve a lot of searching, comparing, and checking details. The interesting part is that the output doesn’t always need to be a long report. Sometimes you just want a recommendation that reflects your particular constraints, with enough explanation to understand why it makes sense.
